evidence_quotes.quote: Despite the democratisation of water and sanitation through policy, as both a human right and an essential basic need, the provision of access and basic services by the two urban municipalities to meet the needs of the informal settlements remains to say the least minimal, requiring negotiation and a struggle for recognition of tenure by residents.

This study used participant observation and in-depth interviews with 15 women from two informal settlements. The choice to focus on two communities located in different provinces was motivated by the authors’ search for credible information to draw a comparison on the conditions in women’s access to water and sanitation and to look for differences and similarities in their situations.

Residents in both communities responded that informal settlements are identified as temporary shelters and even though some become permanent, with the uncertainty of the status they do not know if they qualify for upgrading and for the infrastructure development that is necessary for more formal service delivery.

The Water Services Department needs to obtain the consent of the owner in order to deliver services and many land owners do not give permission because they are afraid of making the settlement on their land more permanent. A further problem is that the density of settlements, such as Endlovini in Cape Town, is very high. In Banana City, a land ownership struggle between the residents and the land owners, the University of KwaZulu-Natal, had to be won before legitimacy and the right to some basic services was secured.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 10 (p. 62, Access to Water and Sanitation)
evidence_quotes.quote: The women related that at one point in 2004 water was turned off for five months when the University wanted to sell the land to e-Thekwini municipality. Banana City residents employed a human rights lawyer to defend their right to occupation of the land. They won the case, stopping the University from evicting them and also won the sympathy of e-Thekwini municipality who agreed after some deliberation to buy the land in order to make the settlement legal (Interview Banana City, 10 December 2010).

The vast majority of informal dwellers interviewed said that they are excluded from decent sanitation as the needs of the people living there are not considered. Although there are several toilet facilities at Endlovini people do not use them. Tenjie a 37 year-old mother of five explained why people are forced to do this: “There are toilets here but they are closed. They (the municipality) just built them and closed them” (Interview Endlovini, 7 December, 2010).

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community access to drinking/domestic water (communal standpipes/taps, water shut-offs, unpiped showers, wash basins) and sanitation (flush toilets, Urine Diversion systems, locked/broken municipal communal toilets, self-built pit latrines, and reliance on bushes/dunes) in two South African urban informal settlements.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Clearly satisfied, as the study examines post-apartheid municipal governance, South Africa's neo-liberal macro-economic policy (GEAR), municipal 'unfunded mandates', Free Basic Water / Indigent Water policies, local settlement leadership/water forums, and tenure struggles. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Borderline because the paper's headline 'neo-liberalism' (GEAR) framing is macro-governance background (water at communal standpipes in both sites is provided free without restriction), but ultimately satisfied because the qualitative empirical findings directly examine rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms governing service access at the settlement/household level: (1) tenure and legal-status eligibility rules — informal settlements are classified as 'temporary shelters', creating uncertainty over whether residents qualify for upgrading and formal service infrastructure, and municipal Water Services Departments require landowner consent or municipal land purchase before installing services; (2) legal mobilization/enforcement — in Banana City, water was turned off for five months in 2004 during an attempted land sale/eviction by the landowner (University of KwaZulu-Natal) until residents hired a human rights lawyer, won occupation rights in court, and secured e-Thekwini Municipality's agreement to buy and legalize the land, enabling municipal tap and toilet provision; (3) the gap between tariff-exemption rules (Free Basic Water / City of Cape Town Indigent Water Policy) and unreticulated informal tenure; and (4) municipal administrative locking of built communal toilets in Endlovini.
criterion_notes.c3: Primary qualitative comparative case study based on participant observation and in-depth interviews with 15 women (plus community leader interviews) conducted over six consecutive days (up to four hours per day) in each of two informal settlements (December 2010 to January 2011), translated from Xhosa and Zulu into English and analysed thematically. Per review safeguards, qualitative socio-legal studies with relevant mechanisms are eligible regardless of lacking quantitative effect estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete water and sanitation access and exclusion outcomes: tap-to-household scarcity (e.g. 6 taps for Banana City with 21 families in Section C having no taps or toilets; scattered malfunctioning standpipes in Endlovini), a 5-month water disconnection in Banana City in 2004, long collection distances and queuing/time poverty, exclusion from sanitation due to municipally locked or broken communal toilets in Endlovini forcing open defecation or self-built pit latrines, vs negotiated installation of 8 flush toilets and 62 Urine Diversion toilets in Banana City.
criterion_notes.c5: Population (poor women residents, n = 15 interviewees, plus community leaders in Banana City, Durban and Endlovini, Cape Town; units of analysis: individual women, households, and settlements), rule-type exposure (tenure/legal-status qualification rules, landowner consent, anti-eviction litigation/legalization, indigent free-water rules, municipal locking of facilities), access outcomes, and qualitative comparative case study design are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English (with primary interviews conducted in Xhosa and Zulu and translated into English by the study's research team).

study_design: Qualitative comparative case study (participant observation and in-depth interviews)
population_and_sample: Poor women residents (n = 15 in-depth interviewees; mean age 35, mean household size 6) and community leaders in two urban informal settlements in South Africa: Banana City in Durban (e-Thekwini Municipality, KwaZulu-Natal) and Endlovini (Monwabisi Park) in Khayelitsha, Cape Town (Western Cape); units of analysis are individual women, households, and informal settlements.
exposure: Tenure insecurity and legal/administrative rules governing informal settlement service access — including 'temporary shelter' classification creating uncertainty over qualification for upgrading and formal infrastructure, landowner-consent requirements for municipal service delivery, anti-eviction litigation and municipal land purchase to legalize settlement tenure, Free Basic Water / Indigent Water policies in unreticulated settlements, and municipal locking of communal toilets — framed within municipal 'unfunded mandates' and neo-liberal policy.
outcome: Household and settlement-level water and sanitation access and exclusion, including availability and functionality of communal standpipes/taps and toilets (flush toilets, Urine Diversion systems, self-built pit latrines, and locked/broken municipal toilets), a 5-month water shut-off during an eviction/land-sale dispute, collection walking distance and queuing time burden, and open defecation with associated health and safety risks for women.
rationale: Full-text qualitative comparative case study (participant observation and 15 in-depth interviews across Banana City in Durban and Endlovini in Cape Town) examining women's household and community access to water and sanitation in informal settlements. Although the overarching 'neo-liberalism' (GEAR) framing is macro-governance background (communal standpipe water is provided free without restriction under municipal Free Basic Water / Indigent policies in both settlements), the primary empirical findings directly examine rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms governing service access under Criterion 2: temporary-shelter administrative status creating uncertainty over upgrading/infrastructure qualification, landowner-consent rules blocking municipal water/sanitation installation on non-municipal land, a 5-month water disconnection in Banana City resolved through anti-eviction litigation and municipal agreement to purchase and legalize the land, limits of Free Basic Water / Indigent policies without legal tenure and reticulation infrastructure, and municipal locking of communal toilets in Endlovini. Satisfies all review inclusion criteria (c1–c6) for qualitative mechanism synthesis.
